title: The Tree of Five
voice: Lūyī to his friends: a plain-spoken teacher who scoffs, commands and bears witness, in the child-prophet plainness of Blake's Songs.
refrainCue: Make it firm, and measure great bliss

lines.en: The body's a fine tree; its branches are five.
Death has come into the restless mind.
Make it firm, and measure great bliss:
ask the guru and know. Lūyī says this.
What do all the samādhis do?
Through pleasure and pain you die, it's true.
From the bonds of metre, from hope in the rules of practice, cut loose;
press close to the side of emptiness, friends, and take up the noose.
Lūyī says: in meditation I have seen;
dhamaṇa, camaṇa, the two, I made my seat.

couplets.kept: The tree, its five branches, Death getting into the mind; a vowel rhyme on five / mind for the source's ḍāla / kāla.
couplets.letGo: 'Fine tree' keeps taruvara's praise but not its sound.

couplets.kept: Perfect rhyme on bliss / this, as on parimāṇa / jāṇa; the refrain short enough to sing back after every couplet.
Perfect rhyme on do / true for kariai / mariāi; the scoff at samādhis left as a question with no answer.
couplets.letGo: 'Certainly' becomes 'it's true', a spoken shrug more than a verdict.

couplets.kept: The one half-line the source makes too long for its metre is too long here too; perfect rhyme on loose / noose, as on āsa / pāsa.
couplets.letGo: 'Let go of' becomes 'cut loose from', which is harder.

couplets.kept: Lūyī's signature and what he saw, in the source's order.
couplets.letGo: The source leaves this couplet unrhymed; seen / seat chimes a little.

note: An example made with Claude to show the Blake lens; unreviewed.
